meta.name: Sovereign IQ
meta.disclaimer: This executive diagnostic provides directional technical sovereignty and regulatory defensibility analysis. It does not constitute legal counsel.

pillars.name: Data Sovereignty & Localization
pillars.desc: Data at rest, in transit, and in-memory residency across borders.

pillars.name: Jurisdictional Reach & Extraterritoriality
pillars.desc: Exposure to foreign subpoenas, CLOUD Act reach & conflict of laws.

pillars.name: Operational & Personnel Sovereignty
pillars.desc: Local clearance, 24/7 follow-the-sun admin bounds & out-of-band telemetry.

pillars.name: Cryptographic & Technical Autonomy
pillars.desc: HYOK/External Key Management, HSM isolation & Confidential Computing.

pillars.name: Software, Vendor & Supply Chain Sovereignty
pillars.desc: CTPP concentration, exitability, open standards & hardware provenance.

maturityStages.label: Reactive
maturityStages.desc: Compliance handled ad-hoc and after the fact; cross-border and foreign access exposure largely unmapped.

maturityStages.label: Aware
maturityStages.desc: Obligations identified; residency addressed on paper but operational and jurisdictional controls patchy.

maturityStages.label: Structured
maturityStages.desc: Defined policies and ownership; residency localized, but vendor-held encryption keys and SaaS blindspots remain.

maturityStages.label: Managed
maturityStages.desc: Controls tested and evidenced; HYOK/BYOK deployed, sub-processor chains audited, and exit strategies documented.

maturityStages.label: Sovereign-by-Design
maturityStages.desc: Sovereignty embedded in architecture, procurement & CI/CD; engineered to minimise exposure to extraterritorial access.

regimes.name: Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)
regimes.penalty_rule: Financial entities: administrative penalties and remedial measures set under national law (Art. 50-51), with no EU-wide cap. Critical ICT third-party providers only: periodic penalty payments up to 1% of average daily worldwide turnover (Art. 35(8)).
duties: Board ICT risk governance
Major incident reporting within 4h
Threat-Led Penetration Testing (TLPT) >= 3 yrs
Register of Information for all ICT contracts
Documented & tested exit strategies for critical functions

regimes.name: NIS2 Directive & CER
regimes.penalty_rule: Up to €10M or 2% global turnover for essential entities; €7M or 1.4% for important entities.
duties: Corporate cyber hygiene (MFA, asset inventory, patching)
Supply chain security assessments
24h early warning incident reporting
Direct management body liability for non-compliance

regimes.name: EU AI Act
regimes.penalty_rule: Up to €35M or 7% global turnover (prohibited AI); €15M or 3% (high-risk violations).
duties: Risk management system & data governance for Annex III high-risk AI
Technical documentation & continuous event logging
Human oversight controls & conformity assessment
GPAI provider transparency & copyright policy compliance

regimes.name: EU Data Act
regimes.penalty_rule: Enforced via national DPAs and competent authorities under national fining rules.
duties: Mandatory cloud switching & data portability facilitation
Contractual fairness bars on unilateral data access
Safeguards against unlawful third-country governmental access to non-personal data

regimes.name: EU GDPR
regimes.penalty_rule: Up to €20M or 4% of global annual turnover for Chapter V transfer breaches.
duties: Lawful basis, transparency & data subject rights
Chapter V restrictions on cross-border data transfers
Schrems II Transfer Impact Assessments (TIAs) with supplementary technical measures
Art. 9 strict conditions for special-category personal data

regimes.name: UK GDPR & Data (Use & Access) Act 2025
regimes.penalty_rule: Up to £17.5M or 4% of global annual turnover.
duties: UK GDPR compliance & ICO registration
International Data Transfer Agreement (IDTA) or UK Addendum
Monitoring phased reforms under the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025
PECR compliance for electronic communications

regimes.name: UK Operational Resilience & Outsourcing
regimes.penalty_rule: Supervisory capital add-ons, business restrictions, and public enforcement sanctions.
duties: Identification of Important Business Services (IBS)
Impact tolerance setting under severe-but-plausible disruption
Mapping of supporting people, processes, technology & third parties
Annual board-approved Self-Assessment document

regimes.name: UK Critical Third Parties Regime

regimes.penalty_rule: Disqualification from public sector tenders and defense/critical infrastructure procurements.
duties: Strict immunity from non-EU extraterritorial laws
Data storage, operations, and support 100% within EU by cleared personnel
Custody of encryption keys held by independent EU entity

regimes.name: CRR/CRD & EBA Cloud Outsourcing

duties: Strict restriction on cross-border personal data transfers outside KSA

Localization preference for government and citizen data

regimes.name: KSA NCA ECC & CSCC Frameworks

duties: Data hosting and primary infrastructure must be within KSA boundaries

regimes.name: KSA SAMA Framework & CITC Cloud Regulations

regimes.penalty_rule: Banking operational fines, suspension of financial services, and provider class de-licensing.

Adherence to CST/CITC Cloud Service Provider classifications (Class A/B/C)

Tested disaster recovery inside KSA territory

regimes.name: UAE Federal Personal Data Protection Law

regimes.name: US CLOUD Act Extraterritorial Reach
regimes.penalty_rule: Contempt of court citations and severe criminal penalties for US corporate parents refusing compliance.
duties: Obliges US-headquartered tech firms (and subsidiaries) to provide data under US warrants regardless of physical location

regimes.name: FISA Section 702 & EO 14086
regimes.penalty_rule: Invalidates standard cross-border transfer mechanisms without supplementary technical safeguards.

Drives Schrems II requirement for Supplementary Technical Measures (end-to-end encryption with external keys)
Requires ongoing Transfer Impact Assessment (TIA) review of US cloud hosting

Prohibition on providing data stored within China to foreign judicial/law enforcement without approval

consultingProbes.q: You indicated domestic data localization (EU/KSA/UAE), but host on a US-headquartered hyperscaler without Hold-Your-Own-Key (HYOK). Under the US CLOUD Act, the provider can be legally compelled to decrypt data at the hypervisor level without domestic judicial review. Who formally approves this residual jurisdictional exposure at board level?
options: No formal board approval; assumed physical region selection was sufficient for compliance
Executive risk committee accepted residual risk based on provider SOC2 and contractual clauses
Legal counsel actively reviewing HYOK / External Key Store deployment for 2026 budget
Architecture team planning migration to national sovereign cloud or certified sovereign enclave
consultingProbes.probePrompt: Consultant / Client notes on board risk acceptance, key management roadmaps, or legal counsel positions...

consultingProbes.q: Core corporate workflows rely on enterprise SaaS (M365, Salesforce, ServiceNow) where the vendor manages encryption keys and global SRE support teams operate outside your jurisdiction. If a foreign court issues a production order to the SaaS provider, can you technically prevent disclosure?
options: No technical prevention possible; relying entirely on vendor pushback and notification commitments
Evaluating SaaS Customer Key (e.g. M365 Customer Key / Salesforce Cache Key) to enforce tenant encryption
Considering dedicated on-premises or sovereign private cloud instances for sensitive records
SaaS used solely for non-regulated, non-confidential business communication
consultingProbes.probePrompt: Consultant notes on M365/Salesforce tenant encryption readiness, sub-processor lists, or telemetry opt-outs...

consultingProbes.q: You maintain on-premises data centers, but hardware out-of-band management controllers (iDRAC/iLO) and storage arrays maintain active telemetry and remote maintenance tunnels to foreign vendor support centers. Has this remote firmware and maintenance channel been audited for foreign access risk?
options: Not formally audited; default vendor phone-home and automated firmware update channels remain enabled
Firewalled with strict IP whitelisting, but vendor technicians can initiate sessions during incidents
Active project underway to transition all OOB and storage telemetry to air-gapped management networks
Hardware vendor agreements mandate local national clearance for all remote diagnostics
consultingProbes.probePrompt: Consultant notes on firmware supply chain, out-of-band network isolation, or vendor support agreements...

consultingProbes.q: Under DORA Art. 28, APRA CPS 230, and MAS Outsourcing rules, financial institutions must maintain tested, feasible exit plans from critical ICT third parties. You reported severe single-vendor concentration with an exit timeline exceeding 6–18 months. When was an actual operational cutover or live exit drill last simulated?
options: Never tested in practice; exit strategy exists solely as a high-level theoretical policy document
Desktop walkthrough conducted within last 12 months; no actual technical cutover or data migration tested
Disaster recovery tested annually within the same hyperscaler, but alternative provider migration untested
Active multi-cloud / container portability project budgeted to reduce single-vendor dependency
consultingProbes.probePrompt: Consultant notes on Register of Information status, CTPP alternative provider feasibility, or legacy lock-in...

consultingProbes.q: While primary production data is localized domestically, secondary disaster recovery, snapshot archives, or database replication traverse national borders. In jurisdictions with strict localization (KSA, India, UAE, Russia), this secondary flow represents a statutory breach. Is replication encrypted with independent domestic keys?
options: Replication uses cloud-native encrypted pipes, but secondary region sits in a foreign jurisdiction without domestic KMS
Legal counsel cleared regional replication under existing international data transfer mechanisms
Currently re-architecting backup policies to force local secondary availability zones
Disaster recovery data is fully pseudonymized / tokenized prior to cross-border replication
consultingProbes.probePrompt: Consultant notes on backup data flows, secondary storage locations, or cross-border network topologies...

consultingProbes.badge: Reclassification: EU AI Act & GPAI Risk
consultingProbes.q: Under EU AI Act Art. 25, an enterprise integrating a third-party General Purpose AI model (e.g. OpenAI, Anthropic) into a high-risk workflow can be legally reclassified as an AI Provider — bearing full conformity and technical documentation obligations. Have you secured the vendor technical provenance files and training data summaries?
options: No provenance files secured; deploying third-party commercial APIs under standard enterprise terms
Conducting fundamental rights and data governance impact assessments prior to production rollout
Restricting high-risk decisions to human-in-the-loop validation with automated model audit logging
Transitioning to self-hosted open-weight models (Llama, Mistral) in local confidential cloud enclaves
consultingProbes.probePrompt: Consultant notes on AI model inventory, high-risk use cases, or AI Office compliance readiness...

questions.q: Where is your primary production data physically stored and hosted at rest?

Contract terms unexamined / default click-through enterprise agreement

Partially — Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) signed, but formal surveillance analysis incomplete

Customer Approval Required: Provider support requires Just-In-Time (JIT) customer approval and access broker logging
Standard Follow-the-Sun: Global support engineers access environments based on timezone rotations

questions.q: For on-premises hardware, storage, and firewalls, are remote out-of-band management channels (iDRAC/iLO) active?
questions.hint: Hardware vendor call-home telemetry and remote support tunnels represent unmapped extraterritorial vectors.

opts.text: Air-gapped / Strictly internal OOB networks with all vendor phone-home telemetry blocked
Connected OOB networks with automated vendor telemetry and remote diagnostics enabled
No on-premises infrastructure / Pure Cloud

questions.q: In SaaS applications (M365, Salesforce, ServiceNow), does the SaaS provider hold administrative access to tenant data?
questions.hint: Most enterprise SaaS platforms operate multi-tenant databases where vendor SREs possess broad diagnostic privileges.

opts.text: Customer Lockbox enforced: Vendor engineers cannot access tenant data without explicit time-limited approval
Standard SaaS operations: Provider manages uptime and internal access under standard security attestations (SOC2)
Uncontrolled / Multi-tenant SaaS with unmonitored vendor telemetry feeds

questions.q: How are encryption keys managed for data at rest across your public cloud and SaaS environments?
questions.hint: If the cloud provider holds or has access to your encryption keys, encryption does NOT defeat foreign subpoenas.

opts.text: Hold Your Own Key (HYOK) / External HSM: Keys generated, stored, and managed in on-prem or sovereign HSMs
Bring Your Own Key (BYOK): Customer imports keys into cloud-managed KMS (provider can access during operations)
Cloud Provider-Managed Keys: Default server-side encryption with provider-owned keys (AWS SSE-S3, Azure PMK)

questions.q: Have you implemented Confidential Computing (hardware-rooted enclaves e.g. AMD SEV-SNP, Intel SGX) for data in use?
questions.hint: Confidential Computing protects data in memory from hypervisor inspection and rogue administrative access.

opts.text: Yes — Deployed in production for high-risk data processing and AI inference
Evaluating / PoC — Testing confidential VMs for regulated financial or healthcare workloads
No — Standard virtualization and container runtimes only

questions.q: Can your organization instantly revoke encryption keys to render foreign-hosted data permanently unreadable?
questions.hint: The definitive technical test of cryptographic sovereignty: remote cryptographic kill-switch.

opts.text: Yes — Cryptographic kill-switch verified: revoking key access instantly blinds all cloud/SaaS data stores
Partial — Can disable keys in cloud console, but cached keys or provider backups may persist
No — Provider manages the lifecycle; instantaneous unilateral revocation is impossible

questions.q: Do you have single-vendor concentration where a disruption to one cloud or SaaS provider halts core business operations?
questions.hint: A primary focus of DORA Art. 28, UK CTP, APRA CPS 230, and MAS Outsourcing guidelines.

opts.text: Severe Concentration: Single hyperscaler / SaaS platform hosts >75% of all critical business functions
Managed Concentration: Dominant primary provider, but critical workloads have documented fallback options
Architectural Multi-Cloud / Hybrid: Workloads portable across distinct providers and on-premises enclaves

questions.q: What is your realistic, tested timeline to execute a complete exit strategy from your primary cloud provider?
questions.hint: Regulatory requirements mandate an actionable, auditable, and tested exit strategy without disruption.

opts.text: Under 3 Months: Workloads are containerized (Kubernetes/OpenShift) and data formats are open standard
6 to 12 Months: Documented transition plan exists, but significant proprietary PaaS rewrites would be required
Over 18 Months / Effectively Impossible: Deep proprietary serverless and database lock-in prevents migration

questions.q: For on-premises hardware, appliances, and telecom equipment, have you audited hardware provenance (e.g. NDAA Section 889)?
questions.hint: National security rules in the US, UK, Australia, and EU ban certain foreign-manufactured telecom and compute components.

opts.text: Fully Audited: Hardware bill of materials (SBOM/HBOM) verified compliant with clean supply chain lists
Partially Audited: Major server vendors certified, but network switches, cameras, and IoT unverified
Not Audited: Hardware procurement driven purely by commercial cost with no origin restrictions
